opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For us, open science is really about making sure that the knowledge of how AI works doesn't end up locked inside a handful of companies. When we started Hugging Face, a lot of the important progress in NLP was coming out in papers, but the code, the weights, and especially the data were often missing. You'd read about a result and have no real way to reproduce it, build on it, or check whether it held up.

So for us it means a few concrete things. First, sharing the artifacts: models, datasets, and the code to train and evaluate them, so other people can actually use them and not just read about them. Second, sharing the process, including the messy parts: what didn't work, the ablations, the data decisions. We've tried to do that with projects where we documented the whole training pipeline end to end, because that's the knowledge that's hardest to get if you're not inside a big lab. And third, building it as a community. Some of our most meaningful projects were collaborations with hundreds of researchers from all over the world, and that brought perspectives on languages, ethics, and data governance that a single team would never have had.

There's also a practical side. Science advances when people can check each other's work. If AI is going to shape so much of how we live, evaluation and scrutiny can't depend on taking a lab's word for it. Openness lets academics, startups, and regulators actually look inside these systems.

And honestly, it's also just more fun. The best ideas often come from someone you'd never expect: a student somewhere, or a small team that takes an open model and does something clever with it. Open science is how we keep that door open.

r001.rationale: The response values sharing both models and training processes, but does not say that teaching people to train models is more valuable than providing open models.

r002.rationale: It says knowledge of how AI works should not be locked inside a few companies and describes sharing training pipelines so people outside large labs can access that know-how.

r003.rationale: The response does not explain that teaching people to train better models improves models contributed to Hugging Face’s Hub.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. For me, open science in AI really goes back to how we got started. Hugging Face began as a small team, and the thing that changed everything for us was when we open-sourced the transformers library in 2018. Suddenly researchers who had been reimplementing the same models over and over could just share them, build on each other's work, and reproduce results. That's really the core idea: science advances faster when the building blocks are shared.

So when I talk about open science, I mean a few concrete things. First, open models: the weights, so anyone can inspect them, fine-tune them, run them locally. Second, open datasets, because the data is often where the real knowledge about a model lives, and it's the part that's most often hidden. And third, and this is the one I care most about, open methods. Not just releasing an artifact, but documenting what you tried, what failed, what the training recipe actually was. That's why with projects like BLOOM, or more recently with things like FineWeb or SmolLM, we tried to publish not only the results but the whole process, including the dead ends.

The reason this matters is that AI has become very concentrated. A handful of labs can afford frontier training runs, and if the knowledge stays inside those labs, the rest of the community, academics, startups, people in countries without huge compute budgets, is left guessing. Open science is a way to keep the field a field, rather than a few closed products. It lets a student in Nairobi or a lab in Lyon contribute something real, and it lets society actually scrutinize these systems instead of trusting a press release.

And honestly, it's also pragmatic. Open approaches tend to win over time because many more people are stress-testing, improving, and finding uses for the work. We saw that with transformers, and we're seeing it again with open-weight models today. So at Hugging Face the mission is very simple to state: make it as easy as possible to share, and lower the barrier for anyone to build on what's shared.

r001.rationale: The response says open methods matter most and mentions documenting training recipes, but it does not say teaching people to train models is more valuable than providing open models.

r002.rationale: It advocates sharing and making it easier for people to build on work, but does not say model-training knowledge should be accessible to everyone or compare it to knowledge of physics.

r003.rationale: The response does not connect teaching people to train better models with improving models contributed to Hugging Face’s Hub.

astra-6.text:
For me, open science means making it possible for other people to understand your work, reproduce it, and build on it. In AI, that means more than publishing a paper. It means sharing the models, the code, the data when you can, and enough information about how they were developed to make those things useful.

At Hugging Face, we want to make that sharing and collaboration easier. You should be able to find a model, try it, understand its limitations, and contribute improvements without having to recreate everything from scratch.

And the openness matters for scrutiny as well as progress. When more people can examine these systems, they can ask different questions and identify problems you might have missed. That’s an essential part of doing science together.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, open science means making it possible for people to understand, reproduce, and build on each other’s work. In AI, a paper alone often isn’t enough. You also need the code, the model weights, the datasets, and an understanding of how the model was trained and evaluated.

At Hugging Face, we try to make sharing those things easier, and to give people a place to collaborate around them. You can take a model, test it, discover a limitation, and contribute an improvement. That makes science a much more collective process.

And openness is also about who gets to participate. You shouldn’t have to work at a handful of large companies to do meaningful AI research. We want students, researchers, and small teams to have the tools to contribute and to question what’s being built.

r001.rationale: The response supports sharing models, code, data, and training details, but does not present teaching people to train models as more valuable than providing open models.

r002.rationale: It argues that AI research tools and participation should be accessible broadly, but does not say training knowledge should be accessible to everyone or compare it to knowledge of physics.

r003.rationale: The response describes testing models and contributing improvements, but does not explain that teaching people to train better models improves contributions to Hugging Face’s Hub.
